meta.titre: Atomic and nuclear physics: nucleus, radiations and half-life
meta.sous_theme: Structure of the atom, radioactivity and half-life

sections.contenu_markdown: Doctors in Yaounde use a radioactive tracer to check how the thyroid gland works, and the smoke alarms in some large buildings contain a tiny radioactive source. Radioactivity is useful but dangerous, so you must know what the radiations are, how far they travel and how quickly a source loses its strength. At the GCE you are asked for the particles in the nucleus, the nature of alpha, beta and gamma radiation, the meaning of half-life, and a simple decay or half-life calculation.

items: An atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by negatively charged electrons.
Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.
Halving a quantity repeatedly gives the sequence $\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{4}, \dfrac{1}{8}, \dots$

sections.titre: The nucleus, radioactive decay and half-life
sections.contenu_markdown:
**The nucleus** contains protons (charge $+1$, mass 1 unit) and neutrons (no charge, mass 1 unit), together called nucleons. Electrons (charge $-1$, negligible mass) move outside the nucleus. A nuclide is written ${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}$, where $A$ is the nucleon (mass) number $=$ protons $+$ neutrons, and $Z$ is the proton (atomic) number. So neutrons $= A - Z$. Isotopes are atoms of the same element (same $Z$) with different numbers of neutrons.

**Radioactivity** is the spontaneous and random disintegration of an unstable nucleus, with emission of radiation. It is not changed by heating, pressure or chemical combination.

| Radiation | What it is | Charge | Stopped by | Ionising power |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Alpha ($\alpha$) | helium nucleus ${}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ | $+2$ | thick paper, a few cm of air | strongest |
| Beta ($\beta$) | fast electron ${}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$ | $-1$ | a few mm of aluminium | medium |
| Gamma ($\gamma$) | electromagnetic wave | none | several cm of lead | weakest |

**Decay rules.** In alpha decay the nucleus loses 2 protons and 2 neutrons: $A$ falls by 4 and $Z$ by 2. In beta decay a neutron changes into a proton and an electron: $A$ stays the same and $Z$ rises by 1. Gamma emission changes neither $A$ nor $Z$. In every equation the totals of $A$ and of $Z$ must be equal on both sides.

**Half-life** is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample (or for the count rate to fall to half). After $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$. Subtract the **background count** before you apply half-lives.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a question asks you to complete a nuclear equation
variantes.contenu_markdown:
Alpha decay of radium: ${}^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} \to {}^{222}_{86}\mathrm{Rn} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$. Check: $226 = 222 + 4$ and $88 = 86 + 2$.

Beta decay of carbon-14: ${}^{14}_{6}\mathrm{C} \to {}^{14}_{7}\mathrm{N} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$. Check: $14 = 14 + 0$ and $6 = 7 + (-1)$.

Find the daughter nuclide by balancing $A$ first, then $Z$, and read its name from the new value of $Z$ in the periodic table.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when a table or numbers of half-lives are given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Method: (1) correct the reading by subtracting the background count; (2) divide the elapsed time by the half-life to get $n$; (3) divide the corrected count rate by $2^n$. Add the background again only if the question asks for what the counter would actually read. A half-life is the same for any starting amount, and it is fixed for a given nuclide.

variantes.quand_utiliser: when asked to give a use of radiation or a safety precaution
variantes.contenu_markdown: Uses: gamma rays sterilise surgical instruments and treat cancer; beta particles control the thickness of paper or metal foil (the reading changes with thickness); alpha sources are used in smoke alarms; tracers with a short half-life are used in medicine; long half-life nuclides date old rocks and wood. Dangers: radiation ionises and damages living cells. Precautions: store sources in lead-lined containers, handle them with tongs, keep a distance, limit the time of exposure and wear badges that record the dose.

sections.enonce_markdown: A radioactive source has a half-life of 12 minutes. A Geiger counter placed near it, with the source absent, records a background count rate of $30$ counts per minute. With the source in place it records $510$ counts per minute. (a) What is the count rate due to the source alone? (b) What will the counter read for the source and background together after $36$ minutes?

etapes.action: Subtract the background from the reading.
etapes.justification: Only the source decays; the background is always present and does not change.
Number of half-lives is elapsed time divided by half-life.

etapes.action: Halve the source count rate three times.
etapes.justification: Each half-life halves the count rate of the source.
The counter measures source plus background.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The source alone gives $480$ counts per minute at the start and $60$ counts per minute after $36$ minutes. The counter reads **90 counts per minute**.

items.erreur_markdown: The mass number of an atom is the number of protons in its nucleus.
items.pourquoi_faux: The proton number $Z$ counts the protons. The mass (nucleon) number $A$ counts protons and neutrons together.
items.correction_markdown: Neutrons $= A - Z$. For ${}^{23}_{11}\mathrm{Na}$ there are 11 protons and $23 - 11 = 12$ neutrons.

items.erreur_markdown: Beta particles come from the electrons in the outer shells of the atom.
items.pourquoi_faux: Beta particles come from the nucleus. A neutron changes into a proton and a fast electron, which is emitted. That is why $Z$ increases by 1 while $A$ is unchanged.
items.correction_markdown: Write the beta particle as ${}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$ and increase $Z$ by 1 in the daughter nucleus.

items.erreur_markdown: Half-life is half the time the sample takes to disappear completely, so the sample is finished after two half-lives.
items.pourquoi_faux: Half-life is the time for half of the nuclei present to decay. After one half-life $\tfrac{1}{2}$ is left, after two $\tfrac{1}{4}$, and so on. The amount never reaches zero in a simple calculation.
items.correction_markdown: Use $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$ with $n$ the number of half-lives.

items.erreur_markdown: Using the raw counter reading in a half-life calculation.
items.pourquoi_faux: The reading includes background radiation from rocks, air and cosmic rays. It does not halve with the source, so halving the raw reading gives a wrong result.
items.correction_markdown: Subtract the background count first, halve the corrected value, and add the background again if the reading is asked for.

items.erreur_markdown: Alpha particles are the most penetrating radiation because they are the heaviest.
items.pourquoi_faux: Alpha particles are large and carry a double charge, so they collide with air molecules and are stopped within a few centimetres or by thick paper. Gamma rays are the most penetrating.
items.correction_markdown: Order of penetration: alpha $<$ beta $<$ gamma. Order of ionising power: alpha $>$ beta $>$ gamma.

items.enonce_markdown: A uranium nuclide ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ emits an alpha particle. (a) How many protons and neutrons does the uranium nucleus contain? (b) Write the nuclide produced, in the form ${}^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Protons $= Z = 92$. Neutrons $= A - Z = 238 - 92 = 146$. **92 protons and 146 neutrons.**

(b) Alpha emission: $A$ falls by 4 and $Z$ by 2, so $A = 234$ and $Z = 90$ (thorium). **${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$**, and the equation is ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \to {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.

items.enonce_markdown: Cobalt-60, ${}^{60}_{27}\mathrm{Co}$, decays by emitting a beta particle, followed by gamma radiation. (a) State the number of protons and neutrons in the cobalt nucleus. (b) Write the nuclear equation for the beta decay. (c) State the number of neutrons in the daughter nucleus and say what the gamma emission changes.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Protons $= 27$; neutrons $= 60 - 27 = 33$. **27 protons, 33 neutrons.**

(b) Beta decay: $A$ unchanged, $Z$ rises by 1, so the daughter has $A = 60$, $Z = 28$ (nickel). **${}^{60}_{27}\mathrm{Co} \to {}^{60}_{28}\mathrm{Ni} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}$**. Check: $27 = 28 + (-1)$.

(c) Neutrons in nickel-60: $60 - 28 = 32$. **32 neutrons.** Gamma emission removes surplus energy from the nucleus and **changes neither $A$ nor $Z$**.

items.enonce_markdown: A source has a half-life of $8$ days. Its count rate is $800$ counts per minute at the start; background radiation can be ignored. (a) What is the count rate after $32$ days? (b) After how many days will the count rate be $25$ counts per minute? (c) A factory wants to monitor the thickness of paper as it comes out of a machine. Which radiation (alpha, beta or gamma) should the source emit, and why?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $n = \dfrac{32}{8} = 4$ half-lives. $800 \div 2^4 = 800 \div 16$, so **50 counts per minute**.

(b) $800 \div 25 = 32 = 2^5$, so 5 half-lives are needed: $5 \times 8$, so **40 days**.

(c) **Beta.** Alpha particles would be completely stopped by even thin paper, so nothing could be measured beyond it. Gamma rays would pass through almost unchanged, so a change in thickness would not alter the reading. Beta particles are partly absorbed by paper, so the count rate changes with the thickness.

items_markdown: The nucleus contains **protons and neutrons** (nucleons). $A = $ protons $+$ neutrons, $Z = $ protons, and neutrons $= A - Z$.
**Alpha** (helium nucleus, $+2$) is stopped by paper; **beta** (fast electron) by a few mm of aluminium; **gamma** (electromagnetic wave) is reduced only by thick lead.
In decay equations the sums of $A$ and of $Z$ balance. Alpha: $A - 4$, $Z - 2$. Beta: $A$ same, $Z + 1$. Gamma: no change.
**Half-life** is the time for half of the radioactive nuclei (or the count rate) to decay. After $n$ half-lives the fraction left is $(1/2)^n$.
Always subtract the **background count** before using half-lives.
